title: 5.4 Reaction Enthalpy (ΔᵣH)
synopsis:
The enthalpy change that accompanies a reaction is the reaction enthalpy, ΔrH:

ΔrH = Σ ai H(products) − Σ bi H(reactants) (Eq. 5.14)

Industry needs it to plan heating or cooling, and it is also needed for the temperature dependence of K. This section covers standard states, phase changes, enthalpy of formation, thermochemical equations and Hess's law.

children.title: ΔᵣH = ΣH(products) − ΣH(reactants)
children.synopsis:
The ai and bi are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation, and Hm is the molar enthalpy.

Example: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)

ΔrH = [Hm(CO2) + 2Hm(H2O,l)] − [Hm(CH4) + 2Hm(O2)]

Uses: planning the heating or cooling needed to keep an industrial reaction at constant temperature, and calculating how the equilibrium constant changes with temperature.

questions.q: Knowledge of Δ_rH is needed for all EXCEPT:
o: Planning heating/cooling of an industrial reaction
Temperature dependence of the equilibrium constant
Predicting the rate constant of a reaction
questions.e: Rate constants belong to chemical kinetics. NCERT lists the other uses.

children.title: (a) Standard Enthalpy & Standard State
children.synopsis:
Enthalpy depends on conditions, so we fix standard ones.

Standard enthalpy of reaction (ΔrH°): the enthalpy change when all participants are in their standard states.

Standard state of a substance at a given temperature: its pure form at 1 bar.

  • Liquid ethanol at 298 K: pure liquid ethanol at 1 bar.
  • Solid iron at 500 K: pure iron at 1 bar.

Data are usually quoted at 298 K. Standard conditions are shown by the superscript °.
traps: The standard state specifies PRESSURE (1 bar), not temperature. A standard state can exist at any temperature; 298 K is just the usual choice.

questions.q: The standard state of a substance at a specified temperature is:
o: Its pure form at 1 atm and 273 K
Its most stable form at 298 K only
questions.e: NCERT: the standard state is the pure form at 1 bar at the specified temperature.

children.title: (b) Enthalpy of Phase Transformations
children.synopsis:
Phase changes happen at constant temperature (and pressure), and they still involve energy.

TermProcess (1 mol, standard state)Example
ΔfusH°solid → liquidIce: 6.00 kJ mol⁻¹ at 273 K
ΔvapH°liquid → vapour (at Tb, 1 bar)Water: +40.79 kJ mol⁻¹
ΔsubH°solid → vapour directlyDry ice: 25.2 kJ mol⁻¹ at 195 K; naphthalene: 73.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  • Melting, vaporisation and sublimation are all endothermic, so these enthalpies are positive. The reverse processes (freezing, condensation) release the same amount.
  • The magnitude depends on intermolecular forces. Water has strong H-bonds and acetone weaker dipole–dipole forces, so acetone needs less heat per mole to vaporise.
  • Since the paths are equivalent (Hess), ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH at the same temperature.

Problem 5.7: 18 g of water on a swimmer at 298 K (ΔvapH = 44.01 kJ mol⁻¹) needs 44.01 kJ. Then ΔvapU = 44.01 − RT = 44.01 − 2.48 = 41.53 kJ.

Problem 5.8: 1 mol of water at 100 °C → ice at 0 °C. ΔH = −(18 × 4.2 × 100) J − 6.00 kJ = −7.56 − 6.00 = −13.56 kJ mol⁻¹. The volume change is negligible, so ΔU ≈ ΔH.

questions.q: Which is true for all enthalpies of fusion and vaporisation?
o: They are zero at the transition temperature
They are equal for all substances
questions.e: Melting and vaporising need heat (endothermic), so these enthalpies are positive.

questions.q: Acetone needs less heat per mole than water to vaporise because:
o: Acetone has a higher molar mass
Water has strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds
questions.e: Strong H-bonding in water holds the molecules tightly. Acetone has only weaker dipole–dipole forces.

questions.q: If ΔfusH = 6.0 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔvapH = 45.0 kJ mol⁻¹ for a substance at the same temperature, its ΔsubH is:
questions.e: Solid → vapour = solid → liquid → vapour, so ΔsubH = 6.0 + 45.0 = 51.0 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.q: During melting of ice at 273 K and 1 atm, the temperature:
questions.e: Phase changes take place at constant temperature; the heat absorbed is latent heat.

children.title: (c) Standard Enthalpy of Formation
children.synopsis:
ΔfH°: the standard enthalpy change for forming one mole of a compound from its elements in their most stable states (reference states).

Reference state of an element is its most stable form at 25 °C and 1 bar: H2(g), O2(g), C(graphite), S(rhombic).

NCERT examples: ΔfH° of H2O(l) = −285.8, CH4(g) = −74.81, C2H5OH(l) = −277.7 kJ mol⁻¹.

Convention: ΔfH° of an element in its reference state = 0.

These are NOT formation enthalpies:

  • CaO(s) + CO2(g) → CaCO3(s), ΔrH = −178.3 kJ: formed from compounds, not elements.
  • H2(g) + Br2(l) → 2HBr(g): two moles formed. Halve it to get ΔfH°(HBr) = −36.4 kJ mol⁻¹.

NCERT erratum: for H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr the text prints ΔrH° = −178.3 kJ mol⁻¹ (copied from the CaCO₃ line). The consistent value is 2 × (−36.4) = −72.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
points: ΔfH° of an element in its most stable form is 0 (e.g. O₂(g), C(graphite)).
ΔfH° of C(diamond) or O₃(g) is NOT zero, because they are not reference states.
traps: ΔfH°(Br₂, l) = 0 but ΔfH°(Br₂, g) ≠ 0, because liquid is bromine's reference state.

questions.q: The enthalpies of all elements in their standard (reference) states are:
questions.e: By convention ΔfH° = 0 for every element in its most stable state at 1 bar.

questions.q: For which substance is ΔfH° NOT zero?
questions.e: Diamond is not carbon's reference state; graphite is.

questions.q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of formation?
questions.e: It forms 1 mol of HBr from its elements in their reference states. The others start from compounds, make 2 mol, or use diamond.

questions.q: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), ΔrH° = −92.4 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔfH° of NH₃(g) is:
questions.e: The equation makes 2 mol of NH₃, so ΔfH° = −92.4/2 = −46.2 kJ mol⁻¹.

children.title: Using ΔfH° to Find ΔᵣH°
children.synopsis:
ΔrH° = Σ ai ΔfH°(products) − Σ bi ΔfH°(reactants) (Eq. 5.15)

NCERT example: CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g)

ΔrH° = (−635.1) + (−393.5) − (−1206.9) = +178.3 kJ mol⁻¹. The reaction is endothermic, so limestone must be heated to make lime.

Recipe: products minus reactants, each multiplied by its coefficient; elements count as zero.

questions.q: ΔfH° values (kJ mol⁻¹): CO(g) = −110, CO₂(g) = −393, N₂O(g) = 81, N₂O₄(g) = 9.7. ΔrH for N₂O₄(g) + 3CO(g) → N₂O(g) + 3CO₂(g) is:
Given ΔfH°: Fe₂O₃(s) = −824.2, H₂O(l) = −285.83 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔrH° for Fe₂O₃(s) + 3H₂(g) → 2Fe(s) + 3H₂O(l) is about:

children.title: (d) Thermochemical Equations
children.synopsis:
A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation plus its ΔrH, with the physical state (and allotropic form) of every substance written in.

Example: C2H5OH(l) + 3O2(g) → 2CO2(g) + 3H2O(l); ΔrH° = −1367 kJ mol⁻¹

Three conventions:

  1. Coefficients mean moles, never molecules.
  2. ΔrH° refers to the moles as written, and its unit is kJ mol⁻¹, meaning per mole of reaction. Halve the equation and you halve ΔH (−33.3 becomes −16.6 kJ for the Fe2O3 example). So enthalpy is extensive.
  3. Reverse the equation and the sign of ΔH flips. N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 is −91.8 kJ; 2NH3 → N2 + 3H2 is +91.8 kJ.

questions.q: If ΔH for A → B is −x kJ, then ΔH for 2B → 2A is:
questions.e: Reversing flips the sign (+x) and doubling doubles the value: +2x kJ.

questions.q: In a thermochemical equation, the stoichiometric coefficients represent:
questions.e: NCERT convention 1: coefficients are moles, never molecules.

questions.q: Heat released on forming 35.2 g of CO₂ from carbon (ΔcH of C = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹) is:

children.title: (e) Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation
children.synopsis:
Enthalpy is a state function, so ΔH for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or many.

If a reaction takes place in several steps, its standard reaction enthalpy is the sum of the standard enthalpies of the intermediate reactions (at the same temperature).

ΔrH = ΔrH1 + ΔrH2 + ΔrH3 + … (Eq. 5.16)

Why we need it: burning carbon always gives some CO2 along with CO, so ΔrH for C → CO cannot be measured directly.

  1. C(graphite) + O2 → CO2; ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹
  2. CO + ½O2 → CO2; ΔH = −283.0 kJ mol⁻¹
  3. Reverse (2): CO2 → CO + ½O2; ΔH = +283.0
  4. Add (1) and (3): C + ½O2 → CO; ΔH = −110.5 kJ mol⁻¹

Toolkit: equations can be added, subtracted, reversed (flip the sign) and multiplied (scale ΔH), exactly like algebra.

questions.q: Hess's law is a direct consequence of the fact that:
questions.e: ΔH depends only on the initial and final states, so it is the same for any route.

questions.q: C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; CO + ½O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −283.0 kJ. ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂ → CO is:
Why can ΔH for C(graphite) + ½O₂ → CO not be measured directly?
o: Some CO₂ is always formed along with CO
questions.e: NCERT: some CO₂ always forms, so direct measurement is impossible; Hess's law is used instead.

questions.q: Given A → B, ΔH = +20 kJ; B → C, ΔH = −50 kJ; C → D, ΔH = +10 kJ. ΔH for D → A is:
